en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has specialized facial feathers called a crest that help it spot prey in the dense rainforest canopy.
The sampaguita, our national flower, releases its sweet fragrance mostly at night to attract specific moth pollinators in the local environment.
Ifugao farmers build stone-walled rice terraces that follow the natural contour lines of the mountains to prevent soil erosion and manage water flow.
During the Lucban Pahiyas festival, locals decorate homes with kiping, which are colorful, leaf-shaped wafers made from ground rice and natural plant dyes.
National Scientist Angel Alcala pioneered the creation of artificial coral reefs in the Philippines to restore marine biodiversity and protect coastal fish populations.
The narra tree, our national tree, develops a deep taproot system that anchors it firmly against the strong winds of frequent Philippine typhoons.
Historically, Filipinos extracted strong fibers from the abaca plant stalk to weave Manila ropes that resisted saltwater damage in maritime trade.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to cool its body because it lacks sufficient sweat glands to regulate heat in tropical climates.
The mangrove forests in Manila Bay have dense, tangled root systems that naturally filter water pollutants and protect the coastline from storm surges.
T'boli artisans use natural dyes extracted from the roots and leaves of local plants to color the threads of their traditional t'nalak cloth.
The bangus, our national fish, thrives in brackish water ponds because its specialized gills allow it to adapt to both saltwater and freshwater environments.
National Scientist Dioscoro Umali developed a system of classifying mango ripeness by observing the skin color and natural chemical changes in the fruit.
